fields.expected: I'd be working on infrastructure for scientific evaluation. Over the past year I've studied how research gets funded and selected, reading the history from patronage to the German research university to Bell Labs to the postwar NIH/NSF project-grant model, and talking with researchers, research administrators, economists, and people building alternative research organizations. I started with the thesis that grant-writing time was the main constraint. I now think the bigger effect is selection: researchers learn which ideas are legible enough to survive review, and never attempt the ones that aren't. The question that came out of that is what happens as AI makes generation cheap. Literature search, coding, analysis, and hypothesis testing are all getting faster, but reviewer time and domain expertise aren't. If generation becomes abundant, judgment becomes the bottleneck. So I'd want to build the technical side of that: methodological validation, provenance and evidence tracing, uncertainty representation, reproducibility checks, and sane escalation to human domain experts. I already got a taste of this at Intelehealth, where I designed an evaluation framework comparing AI-generated clinical outputs against a 4,169-case clinical standard using stratified sampling to surface systematic failure modes. Generating an answer is cheap. Deciding whether to trust it is the hard part.

fields.expected: Estimating sleep without a wearable, for ClarityAtlas. The product only worked if we could tell users something real about their sleep, and requiring a watch would have cut most of our pilot users out. So I built a passive sleep-estimation system on phone-interaction and motion signals, pulling HealthKit and Core Motion inputs like step count, gait speed, and movement patterns. The hard part wasn't the code, it was that I had no clean label. A wearable gives you a signal to fit against; I had absence of activity, which is ambiguous. A phone sitting on a desk during a lecture looks a lot like a phone sitting on a nightstand. I had to decide what evidence was actually sufficient to call a window sleep, and how to behave when it wasn't, because confidently reporting a wrong sleep window is worse for a health product than reporting nothing. That pushed me toward being explicit about uncertainty rather than always producing a number. It also connects to how I built the "Sleep Twins" matching layer on standardized behavioral features and weighted distance, since comparisons are only meaningful if the underlying estimates are honest. We shipped it into a live Hopkins pilot with 30+ users.

fields.expected: How we got our meeting with the Hopkins president. During Lighting of the Quads, my cofounders and I realized Ron Daniels was somewhere nearby. We tracked him to Garland Hall, found the doors locked, could see him through the glass, and just kept knocking until someone let us in and we got a few minutes to pitch Open Health Intelligence. That conversation eventually turned into a formal meeting months later, and we also ended up presenting to leadership from the Data Science and AI Institute. I'm proud of it because my instinct is usually to go build the next thing rather than to go ask someone for something. The project taught me that shipping the product is maybe half the work; recruiting users, getting institutional support, and repeatedly explaining to people why the thing should exist matter just as much. Knocking on a locked door is a small version of that, but it was the moment I stopped treating the non-technical half as someone else's job.

fields.expected: Forward Deployed Software Engineer. The work I've enjoyed most has been the kind where the problem only becomes clear after you're standing in the actual environment. At Intelehealth I built a resource-availability scoring pipeline in Python across 32 villages, combining facility-tier classification, geospatial distances, Google Maps data, weather, and healthcare-resource availability. None of that modeling was interesting in the abstract. It mattered because rural care decisions depend on whether a facility is actually reachable this week. Same with ClarityAtlas: I built the iOS app end to end, but the thing that shaped it most was running a live pilot with 30+ Hopkins users and finding out which metrics people ignored. I also think a lot about where automation should stop. In my job-application agent I deliberately made free-text and demographic fields architecturally unfillable, because a wrong autonomous action there is unrecoverable. That instinct, figuring out which parts of a workflow a system should own and which a human must keep, seems central to delta work. I'd rather write code against a real operational constraint than a spec someone handed me.
